question: Do doctors judge a treatment differently when the same result is given as a relative cut rather than an absolute one?
answer: Yes, markedly. In 1992 Naylor and colleagues showed doctors one trial's results in different forms; they rated the treatment more effective as a relative cut than as the absolute difference or the number needed to treat. The same pills sound bigger as a third fewer heart attacks than as one or two fewer per hundred.
move: Ask for the same result in people per hundred before judging it.
ask: When a deal or a treatment sounds impressive, have I asked to see it in plain counts?
source: Naylor, Chen & Strauss, Annals of Internal Medicine, 1992
reference: Naylor, Chen & Strauss, Measured enthusiasm: does the method of reporting trial results alter perceptions of therapeutic effectiveness?, Annals of Internal Medicine 117:916–921, 1992
